nameStory: This moth earned its "tiger" name from the bold black spots scattered across its white wings, resembling the markings of a tiger's coat. The "Virginian" part of its name comes from Virginia, where early naturalists first documented this species, though it ranges far beyond that state throughout eastern North America.
description: The Virginian Tiger Moth is a medium-sized white moth with distinctive black spots sprinkled across its wings like paint splatters. Adults have a wingspan of about 1.5 to 2 inches and are most active at night, often attracted to porch lights and outdoor fixtures. As caterpillars, they're known as yellow woolly bears - fuzzy, yellow-brown larvae covered in dense, soft hairs. This is one of New England's most commonly observed moths, with over 4,000 sightings recorded in the region.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Pure white or cream-colored wings decorated with scattered black spots of varying sizes, creating a distinctive speckled appearance that looks almost hand-painted

idTips.label: Wing Texture
idTips.description: Wings feel slightly fuzzy to the touch and have a soft, almost velvety appearance rather than the smooth, scale-like texture of many other moths

idTips.label: Body Markings
idTips.description: White to yellowish fuzzy body with black spots along the sides and a notably hairy, almost woolly texture when viewed up close

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with broad, rounded wings that span 1.5-2 inches, giving it a chunky, robust appearance compared to more delicate moths

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are relatively simple and straight, lacking the feathery or club-like appearance of some other moth families

habitat: Virginian Tiger Moths can be found throughout New England in gardens, parks, woodlands, and suburban areas with plenty of vegetation. They prefer areas with diverse plant life since their caterpillars feed on a wide variety of plants including grasses, dandelions, and garden crops. You'll often spot adults around outdoor lights, porch fixtures, and lit windows from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, becoming active as temperatures warm. This is when you might first spot them at porch lights or see the fuzzy yellow caterpillars starting to appear on plants.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period for adults, with moths most commonly seen at lights during warm summer nights. Yellow woolly bear caterpillars are actively feeding and growing during this time.
seasonality.fall: A second generation of adults may emerge in early fall in warmer areas. Caterpillars are preparing for winter by seeking shelter under leaf litter and bark.
seasonality.winter: Adults are absent, but caterpillars overwinter in protected spots like under logs, rocks, or thick leaf litter, emerging to feed on warm winter days.

funFact: The yellow woolly bear caterpillars of this moth are actually beneficial garden helpers - they're like tiny vacuum cleaners that prefer to munch on dandelions, plantain, and other common weeds rather than your prized flowers, making them one of the few caterpillars that many gardeners are happy to see!
confusionNotes: Often confused with the Fall Webworm Moth, which is also white, but Fall Webworms have more elongated wings and their spots tend to be arranged in rows rather than randomly scattered. Remember: Virginian Tigers have "splattered paint" spots, while Fall Webworms have more organized, linear markings.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "tiger" moth, this species belongs to the family Erebidae, not a separate "tiger moth" family. The name "tiger moth" is a common term for several moth groups with bold, contrasting patterns, which can be confusing since they're not all closely related.
compareHints: Since this is the only Spilosoma species in our dataset for New England, compare it to other white moths in the Erebidae family like the Fall Webworm Moth. Virginian Tiger Moths have more randomly scattered spots compared to the more linear or organized patterns of their relatives. Their wings are also broader and more rounded than many similar species, giving them a distinctly chunky appearance.
